newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr settles for caution as Kiwi slides.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr settles for caution as Kiwi slides.

text.p: The Australian dollar faded a little at the midsession as the market tarred it with the same brush as the Kiwi dollar which took a beating this morning.

The New Zealand dollar dived 1/2 cent amid heavy offshore selling, which dealers partly attributed to speculation the weakening economy would ultimately force the RBNZ to sanction this market-led policy easing.

Some of the selling spilled over into the A$, particularly as dealers suspected the risks on rates here were also to the downside despite all the well rehearsed arguments about why this week's cut should be the last of the cycle.
By 12.15 GMT (0215 GMT) the local dollar had settled back at US$0.7450/55 after starting at US$0.7460/65 having firmed from US$0.433/38 late here Thursday.
Dealers said a new trading range seemed to be forming following the break of the old US$0.7310/7440 band with good bids and offers seen either side of US$0.7425 and US$0.7505.
The Kiwi sank to US$0.6449/56 from US$0.6490/97 late Thursday, while the A$ came out the better of the two and pushed to NZ$1.1540/60 from NZ$1.1480/98.
The local currency was also firmer on the yen at 88.31/41 from 87.60/70 and at 58.5 in trade weighted terms from 58.3.

So far the general assumption in the market has been that Wednesday's cut in official rates to 5.00 percent was probably the last of the cycle and, as this became clearer, the dolalr would find more support.
Unfortunately for bulls the data had not been co-operating with this comfortable scenario with both building approvals and retail sales weaker than expected.

And the omens were not proising for next week as private banking data suggested housing finance figures Friday would show a fall in commitments of around 5.0 percent in June on top of a surprise 8.4 percent drop the month before.
Neither were analysts confident July jobs data on Thursday would show the recovery in employment so long anticipated.
Forecasts favour a rise of only around 25,000 in employment which, even combined with June's aenemic 11,900 gain, would still not make up for May's fall of 40,300.

With underlying inflation expected to remain below the RBA's 2-3 percent target range into 1998, the bank would have to have a bias to ease should the economy not show conclusive signs of an acceleration in growth to at least a 4.0 percent clip.
That was not an outlook to inspire bulls.
